planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in part shade to full shade.

directions: This vigorous Proven Winners lady fern selection produces broad, closely spaced pinnae with cresting along the frond margins and a pronounced tasseled tip, giving a fuller and lusher look than the wild species. New fiddleheads unfurl bright green each spring and fill out into a dense, mounded clump useful as a filler in shaded beds and containers. Keep soil evenly moist and rich in organic matter; the plant tolerates summer heat better than many lady fern selections and shows good resistance to rabbit browsing. Leave old fronds in place over winter and cut back in very early spring before new growth reaches about six inches tall.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in low sun to full shade.

directions: 'Rotstiel' means red-stemmed in German, and this crested lady fern selection is named for its bright reddish stipes, which contrast sharply against broad, medium-green, heavily crested fronds tipped with fingered, tassel-like crests. It forms a larger, more dramatic clump than many crested lady ferns, reaching up to several feet tall at maturity in good conditions. Grow in neutral to acidic, loose, richly organic soil kept consistently moist, in low sun to full shade; it is notably deer resistant and well suited to woodland borders, mass plantings, and naturalized shade gardens. Divide congested clumps in early spring as new fiddleheads emerge.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from drying wind.

directions: One of the most storied British fern cultivars, this plumose lady fern was discovered in 1868 by nurseryman R. Moule and later rescued and named by Colonel A. M. Jones after his wife. Its fronds are repeatedly and finely divided, four to five times pinnate, with pinnules slightly overlapping, producing an exceptionally soft, feathery texture that has made it prized among fern collectors for over a century. Grow in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in a sheltered, partially to fully shaded site, as the delicate dissected fronds are prone to windburn and moisture loss in exposed positions. Divide established clumps only when congested, in early spring.

common_name: Lady in Lace Dwarf Crested Lady Fern

planting.note: Plant in moist but well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; a slow grower that takes several years to reach mature size.

directions: A cloned dwarf crested selection from Terra Nova Nurseries, this compact lady fern forms finely divided, lance-shaped fronds that are so heavily frilled and ruffled they resemble a dense patch of curled parsley more than a typical fern. It holds a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit and stays notably smaller than most lady fern cultivars, reaching roughly a foot tall and wide only after several years of slow, steady growth. Grow in acid to neutral, humus-rich soil that stays moist but well drained, in partial to full shade with protection from drying wind. Its small scale suits rock gardens, shaded troughs, and the front of woodland borders where larger ferns would overwhelm the space.
